lesson.title: What Shows Up Most: The Mode and Its Limits
lesson.summary: The mode is the most frequently occurring value in a data set, the only measure of center that works for categorical data, and its behavior connects directly back to unimodal and bimodal shape.
lesson.body:
The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a data set. Unlike the mean and the median, which both require values to be numeric so they can be summed or ordered, the mode can be found for any type of data, including categorical variables like eye color or favorite subject, which makes it the only one of the three standard measures of center that applies outside of quantitative variables. For a quantitative variable it still applies too: it is simply whichever numeric value shows up more often than any other.

Consider eight shoe sizes recorded from a small sample of customers: 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10. Counting occurrences, size 7 appears twice, size 8 appears three times, size 9 appears twice, and size 10 appears once. Size 8 occurs more often than any other value, three times, so the mode of this data set is 8. Notice that the mode does not need any arithmetic at all, no summing, no dividing, no sorting into halves, just a straightforward count of how often each value appears.

The mode connects directly back to the modality concepts covered earlier in this unit: a unimodal distribution has one value or narrow cluster that occurs most often, producing a single peak, while a bimodal distribution has two separate values or clusters that both occur unusually often, producing two peaks. In the earlier shoe-store example under bimodal distributions, sizes 7 and 10 were each the peak of their own local cluster, size 7 among the women's shoes sold and size 10 among the men's, which is exactly a data set with two modes rather than one. A distribution with more than two modes is called multimodal, and a data set where every value appears exactly once, or every value ties for the highest frequency, is often described as having no meaningful mode at all.

The mode has real limitations as a measure of center. It ignores every value except the single most frequent one, or the tied-most-frequent ones, so it can completely disregard the overall pattern of the rest of the data, and for continuous quantitative data, like exact heights measured to the nearest tenth of an inch, it is common for no two values to repeat at all, making the raw mode useless without first grouping the data into intervals. For this reason the mode is used most often for categorical data or for describing the shape of a distribution, as in "unimodal" or "bimodal," rather than as the primary reported measure of center for quantitative data, where the mean and median usually do a better job.

Taken together, mean, median, and mode form a complete toolkit for describing the center of a distribution, each suited to different situations: the mean uses every value but is sensitive to skew and outliers, the median resists outliers by relying only on position, and the mode identifies the single most common value or reveals how many distinct clusters, unimodal, bimodal, or beyond, are present in the data.
